# Global Digital Policy Roundup: June 2026

[Shutterstock](https://www.shutterstock.com/image-photo/image-map-computer-language-over-binary-2467503233)

*The roundup is produced by Digital Policy Alert, an independent repository of policy changes affecting the digital economy. If you have feedback or questions, please contact Maria Buza.*

Overview.The roundup serves as a guide for navigating global digital policy based on the work of the [Digital Policy Alert](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/). To ensure trust, every finding links to the Digital Policy Alert entry with the official government source. The full Digital Policy Alert [dataset](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/activity-tracker) is available for you to access, filter, and download. To stay updated, Digital Policy Alert also offers a customizable [notification service](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/notifications) that provides free updates on your areas of interest. Digital Policy Alert’s [tools](https://clairk.digitalpolicyalert.org/) further allow you to navigate, compare, and chat with the legal text of AI rules across the globe.

Drawing from the Digital Policy Alert’s daily monitoring of developments in the G20 countries, it summarizes the highlights of June 2026 in four core areas of digital policy.

- Content moderation, including the European Parliament and Council's provisional agreement on the Directive on combating child sexual abuse material, the United Kingdom's announcement of planned secondary legislation prohibiting social media services for children under 16, the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court's final thesis on platform liability for third-party content under Article 19 of the Internet Civil Framework, Australia's bill strengthening enforcement of the social media minimum age, and Canada's introduction of the Digital Safety Act.
- AI regulation, including the European Parliament's passage and the Council's adoption of the Digital Omnibus on AI Regulation, the European Commission's proposal for the Cloud and AI Development Act, the signature of the Pax Silica Declaration by ten additional countries, the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity by 35 countries, and the introduction of Russia's bill on supporting the development of AI technologies.
- Competition policy, including the European Commission's preliminary positions that Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure should be designated as gatekeepers under the Digital Markets Act, the General Court's partial annulment of Meta's gatekeeper designation, and the UK Competition and Markets Authority's conduct requirements on Google in general search services.
- Data governance, including Canada's House of Commons' passage of the Lawful Access Act and the introduction of the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, Saudi Arabia's Data Monetisation Policy, South Korea's KRW 624 billion fine imposed on Coupang following a large-scale data breach, and the Irish High Court's judgment upholding the EUR 530 million fine against TikTok and referring questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union.

## **Content moderation**

#### **Europe**

The **European Parliament**and the Council reached a provisional agreement on the [Directive](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/8531) on combating the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child sexual abuse material. The Directive introduces new criminal offenses relating to technological developments, including the design, adaptation, or distribution of AI systems intended to generate child sexual abuse material, paying to access livestreamed child sexual abuse, and the sexual extortion of children. The Council adopted [conclusions](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20107) on preventing and combating cyber violence against girls, recommending that Member States and the European Commission take measures concerning gender-based violence online, including through [design requirements](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20108) for online platforms and infrastructure providers.

Furthermore, the European Commission opened a consultation on draft [guidelines](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19593) for the trusted flagger mechanism under Article 22 of the Digital Services Act and issued the State of the Digital Decade [report](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19909). Additionally, the European Commission and Brazil's National Data Protection Authority signed an [administrative arrangement](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20020) on the protection of children and adolescents in the digital environment.

At the judicial level, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled that Member States [may impose individual age verification measures](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19841) on providers of pornographic content established in other Member States, while general and abstract criminal law obligations cannot be applied to such providers under the e-Commerce Directive. The CJEU also ruled that Member States [may prohibit navigation service operators](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19843) from rebroadcasting roadside check information and issued a judgment on jurisdiction over [personality rights claims](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19896) arising from audiovisual content broadcast on television and the internet.

In **Russia**, the Federation Council adopted a [bill](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19972) amending the Code of Administrative Offenses to introduce fines for violations of the rules governing recommender systems. The bill provides for fines of up to RUB 700,000 for legal entities, and up to RUB 1.4 million for repeat violations, for failing to inform users about recommender systems, publish rules governing their use, or comply with the Federal Service for Supervision of Communications, Information Technology and Mass Media orders.

The **United Kingdom's** Department for Science, Innovation and Technology announced plans for [secondary legislation](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19808) under the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act that would prohibit user-to-user social media platforms from offering services to children under 16, prohibit under-16s from livestreaming, and require AI romantic companion chatbots to enforce a minimum age of 18. The Prime Minister also announced an [initiative](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19700) to require technology companies to implement device-level controls to prevent minors from creating, sharing, receiving, or viewing sexually explicit content, with legislation to be considered if industry implementation is insufficient.

The Office of Communications (Ofcom) published draft amended Illegal Content Codes of Practice for [user-to-user services](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18829) and [search services](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18830), incorporating encouraging or assisting serious self-harm and cyberflashing as priority offenses under the Online Safety Act. Ofcom also proposed [crisis protocol measures](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19753) recommending that providers prepare protocols to manage risks arising from significant increases in illegal or harmful content during crises and maintain dedicated communication channels for law enforcement. Ofcom also published an [open letter](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19756) to online service providers regarding civil unrest in Belfast, recommending the implementation of the crisis protocol before the formal adoption. Furthermore, Ofcom adopted [recommendations](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/16177) on designing for media literacy and issued a [statement](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20135) on the categorization impact assessment under the Online Safety Act. Finally, Ofcom fined [First Time Videos](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/15010) GBP 80,000 for failure to implement highly effective age assurance to prevent children from accessing pornography.

#### **Asia and Australia**

In **Australia**, the [Online Safety Amendment (Strengthening Enforcement for the Social Media Minimum Age) Bill](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20057) was introduced to the House of Representatives. The bill expands the eSafety Commissioner's information-gathering powers to cover age assurance providers and app store providers and increases the maximum penalty for systematic breaches from AUD 49.5 million to AUD 99 million. The eSafety Commissioner issued an [outline](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19633) on safety by design obligations to combat sextortion, highlighting measures including language analysis, classifier tools and removal of image-based abuse material. The Digital Platform Regulators Forum adopted a [memorandum of understanding](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19847) formalizing its operation.

Regarding **enforcement**, the eSafety Commissioner confirmed that [three AI-powered nudifying services](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20006) withdrew from the Australian market following its investigation into their age assurance measures. The Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) filed a lawsuit against [Amazon](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20097) over alleged unfair contract terms related to the introduction of advertising to Prime Video, confirmed that [eDreams](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20056) and [HSK United](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20055) paid fines of AUD 59,400 and AUD 79,200, respectively, over misleading pricing claims, and issued an AUD 19,800 infringement notice to [WeFlex](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19938) over misleading advertising. Lastly, the ACCC issued takedown requests to [Amazon, eBay, Kogan, and Fruugo](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19635) over listings of banned magnet toys and announced that Temu and Gumtree joined the [product safety pledge](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/4753) for e-commerce.

In **China**, the National Cybersecurity Standardization Technical Committee (TC260) opened consultations on [guidelines](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19865) for the security of applications involving minors in cybersecurity and AI technologies and on a [national standard](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19867) on security testing and evaluation methods for critical information infrastructure. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) consulted on a [standard](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19521) on technical requirements for industrial knowledge intelligent computing on industrial internet platforms.

Regarding **enforcement,** the MIIT issued [guidance](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19784) on the management of in-app information windows, prohibiting deceptive or misleading prompts such as shake-activated redirects and requiring companies to conduct self-inspections. The State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) and other departments interviewed [seven third-party train-ticket platforms](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19842) over misleading promotion and the unlawful collection of information.

In **India**, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an order restricting access to [Telegram](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19846) to prevent alleged fraud and misinformation during a national examination period. Additionally, the High Court of Delhi dismissed Telegram's petition challenging the order. The Central Consumer Protection Authority also fined [Physicswallah](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19650) INR 500,000 over the deployment of dark patterns.

In **Indonesia**, the obligation to submit [self-assessment reports](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18761) under the Ministerial Regulation on Child Protection in Electronic Systems came into force. Furthermore, the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs confirmed that electronic system providers, including [Netflix, TikTok, ChatGPT, and Grab](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19761) submitted self-assessment results on age verification measures. Further, [TikTok](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19015) deactivated 4.1 million child accounts, and [YouTube](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18946) removed 600,000 child accounts and launched a digital well-being guidebook in compliance with child protection obligations. The Ministry also issued [findings](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20098) on online gambling-related bot activity targeting social media comment sections.

In **Japan**, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications published a [report](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19664) recommending measures for youth protection in online environments, including default protection measures for young users, strengthened age verification beyond self-declaration, and mandatory requirements for operating system vendors. The Ministry also opened a consultation on a [report](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19857) addressing issues in information distribution in the digital space.

In **South Korea**, several bills amending the Network Act on the [decriminalization of true-fact defamation](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20128), [user speech rights](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20095), [hate information moderation obligations](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19669), and the [preservation of AI-generated labels](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19900) were introduced to the National Assembly. Further bills address [platform operators' liability for hazardous products](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20094) in e-commerce and [age verification](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19976) under the Network Act.

Additionally, the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) adopted an [amendment](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19038) to its guidelines on reviewing labeling and advertising, requiring the disclosure of AI-generated virtual persons used in recommendations and endorsements. Additionally, the Communications Commission and other ministries signed a [memorandum of understanding](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20077) on technical cooperation for deepfake sexual crime response, and the Broadcasting Media and Communications Commission announced the establishment of an [AI crime response inter-agency consultative body](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20069). Lastly, the Commission published the [transparency report](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20125) on illegal filming materials, including sexual deepfake videos and child sexual exploitation materials, covering 83 operators, including Naver, Kakao, Google, and Meta. Regarding enforcement, the FTC rejected an application by [Baemin](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19901) to resolve its investigation into misleading advertising of delivery times through consent decree proceedings and fined [Trip](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19605) KRW 10 million over consumer protection violations in airline ticket sales.

#### **Americas**

Regarding enforcement, the National Data Protection Authority began monitoring [pornographic content providers](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19959), [app stores, and operating system providers](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19824) for compliance with age verification and age assurance requirements under the Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents and launched a [complaints channel](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19671) for reporting violations.

In **Canada**, the Digital Safety Act was introduced to the House of Commons, including [content moderation regulation](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19775), [content moderation authority governance](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19776), [design requirements](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19777), [age verification requirements](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19779), and [user rights](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19780). The Act would require social media operators to make child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate images inaccessible in Canada within 24 hours, submit digital safety plans, and, for AI chatbot operators, publish user guidelines on mitigating harmful content and addressing users expressing suicidal ideation. The accompanying [Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19781) would establish the enforcement authority. Separately, the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture directed the Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission to review its [Canadian programming expenditure framework](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19810) under the Online Streaming Act.

## **Artificial Intelligence**

#### **International cooperation**

At the Second Pax Silica Summit, ten additional jurisdictions, including the European Union, Germany, and Argentina, signed the [Pax Silica Declaration](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20075), bringing the total number of signatories to 24. The Declaration provides for cooperation across the AI supply chain and coordination on measures concerning sensitive technologies. At the same summit, 35 jurisdictions signed the [Joint Statement on AI Opportunity](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20082), setting out shared principles on AI governance, cooperation on AI supply chains, and access to AI computing resources.

#### **Europe**

The **European** Parliament passed, and the Council of the European Union subsequently adopted, the Digital Omnibus on AI Regulation. The Regulation clarifies the [AI Office's competences](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17194) for supervising AI systems based on general-purpose AI models, extends its enforcement powers to AI systems embedded in very large online platforms and search engines, expands access to [AI regulatory sandboxes](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17196), including an EU-level sandbox, and extends SME exemptions to small mid-cap enterprises. The Regulation also amends the AI Act's [design](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17214), [quality of service](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17212), and [cybersecurity](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17213) requirements for high-risk AI systems, the [legal basis for processing special categories of personal data for bias detection](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17195), and the [registration requirements](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17201) for high-risk systems.

The European Commission submitted a proposal for the Cloud and AI Development Act. The proposal introduces four Union assurance levels with cumulative [technical and organizational criteria](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/14100) for cloud computing services to be recognized as providing sovereignty assurance, verified through self-assessment or independent third-party audits, alongside [cybersecurity provisions](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/14101) and [public procurement access rules](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/14103).

The Commission published the draft [Code of Practice](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/16054) on the marking and labeling of AI-generated content under Article 50 of the AI Act and established the [AI Act Advisory Forum](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19598) and the [AI Act Scientific Panel](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/15077). Additionally, the Commission closed its call for evidence on the [review of the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19386), released the [EU Open Source Strategy](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17679), and issued the [Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19649).

**Germany's** Digital Committee approved the [bill](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19773) implementing the EU AI Act. It designates the Federal Network Agency as the primary AI market surveillance authority, while assigning financial sector oversight to the Federal Financial Supervisory Authority. It also requires the establishment of at least one AI regulatory sandbox by 2 August 2026.

In **Russia**, the [bill](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18807) on supporting the development of AI technologies was introduced to the State Duma. It establishes a governance framework for large foundation AI models, including government powers to determine state support measures, mandate the use of sovereign or national models in specific cases, and set risk prevention requirements. The bill also includes [design requirements](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18808), [security requirements](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18816), [copyright protection regulations](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18815), and a [data localization requirement](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18814). Separately, the State Duma rejected a bill on the [mandatory labeling of AI-generated video materials](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17853). Finally, Russia and Vietnam announced a [cooperation agreement](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19944) on emerging technologies.

In the **United Kingdom**, the Ministry of Justice launched the [Legal Services Advisory AI Growth Lab](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19809), a supervised testing environment for AI applications in legal services.

#### **Asia and Australia**

**China’s**Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) issued [implementation opinions](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19837) on the development of AI in the information and communications sector, setting out measures relating to telecommunications, AI infrastructure, sectoral applications, and governance. MIIT also opened a consultation on a [list of selected typical cases of AI applications](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19994), including Huawei Cloud's ModelArts platform for large model industrialization, Baidu's PaddlePaddle deep learning framework, and humanoid and embodied intelligence robot applications from firms such as UBTECH and Leju Intelligent.

In **India**, the Ministry of Communications established a [national working group on AI](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20054) to coordinate AI standardization activities and to support India's participation in international AI standardization processes. Further, the Prime Minister issued a [statement](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19871)on ensuring the safe, rapid, and efficient rollout of AI, "proposing the promotion of safe-by-design AI systems, developing common standards, testing frameworks, and regulatory sandboxes, and strengthening global cooperation against deepfakes, misinformation, and cyber fraud. India concluded agreements with [Slovakia](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19825) covering AI, the Internet of Things, and machine-to-machine applications, and with [South Africa](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19692) on AI and digital infrastructure.**Japan's** Digital Agency adopted [guidelines](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19828) for the procurement and utilization of generative AI in government administration, requiring contracted vendors to meet obligations including incident response procedures, data handling and quality controls, and security measures against prompt injection and denial-of-service attacks.

In **South Korea**, three bills amending the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence were introduced to the National Assembly. The [first bill](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20093) addresses the use of non-personal training data in AI development. The [second bill](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19975) expands the Act's category of AI vulnerable groups to include children and adolescents. The [third bill](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19683) establishes a dedicated governance framework to promote and support the development of physical AI. Additionally, the Ministry of Science and Information and Communication Technology consulted on an [amendment](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19496) to the Enforcement Decree of the Framework Act, which defines AI-vulnerable groups and establishes an AI product and service verification system for public procurement.

## **Competition**

#### **Europe**

The **European Commission** opened consultations on proposed regulations on [multimodal booking](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19760) and [rail ticketing](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19759). The proposals would require multimodal booking services to display products neutrally and online rail ticketing platforms to host products on non-discriminatory terms. The Commission also submitted the proposal for the [Chips Act 2.0](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19646), including measures on eligibility for state aid-compatible support for European semiconductor technology initiatives.

Regarding enforcement, the Commission adopted interim measures requiring [Meta](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17349) to restore and maintain free access to the WhatsApp for Business API for rival general-purpose AI assistants until the conclusion of its investigation. The Commission found that Meta's fee-based access policy was equivalent to an access ban and posed a risk of harm to competition in the AI assistant market.

The Commission reached the preliminary position that [Amazon Web Services](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17167) and [Microsoft Azure](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17169) should be designated as gatekeepers under the Digital Markets Act (DMA) based on their cloud computing services. Further, at the judicial level, the General Court of the European Union issued a ruling partially annulling the [gatekeeper designation of Meta Platforms](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/7765) under the DMA. The Court upheld the designation of Facebook Messenger as a standalone core platform service but annulled the designation of Facebook Marketplace, finding that the Commission had applied an incorrect legal time frame and had not adequately explained why Marketplace still qualified as an online intermediation service following listing restrictions implemented in 2023.

The **Italian**Competition Authority opened an investigation into [Apple](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19875) over alleged violations of the DMA's interoperability provisions. The Authority will investigate whether Apple ensures that third-party consumer cloud providers have free and effective interoperability with iOS and iPadOS on equal terms with Apple’s iCloud. The investigation was opened following complaints submitted in April 2025 and subsequent complaints. The Authority's findings will be shared with the European Commission to support its role as the sole enforcer of the DMA.

The **United Kingdom** Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) imposed conduct requirements on Google following its strategic market status designation in general search services. The [fair ranking requirement](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19854) obliges Google to rank organic search results, including within search generative AI features, based on objective and non-discriminatory criteria and to give publishers advance notice of ranking changes, while further requirements cover [data portability](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19855) and the [use of publisher content](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18021) in general search services.

The CMA also opened consultations on proposed steering conduct requirements for [Apple's](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20142) and [Google's](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20110) mobile platforms, and opened a call for evidence on [near-field communication access conditions](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20112) on Apple's mobile platform. Finally, the CMA consulted on final undertakings pertaining to [Getty Images' acquisition of Shutterstock](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/15155) and opened an investigation into [eBay's proposed acquisition of Depop](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19161).

#### **Asia and Australia**

The **Australian** Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) granted interim authorization to the application store settlement agreement between [Google and Epic Games](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19987) on the basis that the interim conduct is unlikely to reduce competition for Australian users. The ACCC further issued a determination denying authorization for [Screen Producers Australia](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19314) to collectively bargain with streaming services on model contract terms.

In **China**, the State Administration for Market Regulation issued rectification measures against [Lalamove](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19946) pertaining to anti-monopoly compliance, requiring the company to cease algorithmic freight price suppression, refund drivers RMB 120 million in unreasonable fees, cut its commission rate from approximately 11% to approximately 9%, and establish a RMB 50 million driver assistance fund.

In **South Korea**, the [bill](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19951) on audiovisual media services was introduced to the National Assembly. It would repeal the existing broadcasting laws and establish a unified regulatory framework for over-the-top (OTT) services and content-sharing platforms. It sets out obligations regarding service provision, contractual practices, and the use of viewer data, and authorizes the Broadcasting Media and Communications Commission to order corrective measures and impose administrative surcharges for non-compliance. The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) published a [report](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20076) on algorithm-based self-preferencing by digital platforms, finding that artificially favorable ranking increased purchases of a platform's own product by approximately 34% and decreased purchases of the top-ranked competing product by approximately 32%. Regarding enforcement, the FTC rejected applications by [Coupang](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19903) and the operator of [Baemin](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19902) to resolve investigations into alleged most-favored-nation clause demands through consent decree proceedings.

#### **Americas**

**Argentina’s** National Competition Authority approved [Telecom’s acquisition of Telefónica Móviles](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19971), subject to structural and behavioral remedies. Telecom must divest certain mobile, fixed-line, and fiber assets and provide the new operator with access to roaming and infrastructure. The decision also imposes obligations related to non-discrimination, service quality, and wholesale access.

**Brazil's** National Telecommunications Agency (Anatel) announced an inquiry into the Internet of Things and machine-to-machine communications markets. The inquiry will examine business models, connectivity investments, network impacts, and barriers to market entry. The findings will support Anatel's monitoring of wholesale connectivity markets, dispute resolution, and potential future regulation to promote competition.

#### **Africa**

The Competition Commission of **South Africa** closed its consultation on the [review of regulations](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19190) that may restrict competition and the entry or expansion of firms, with a particular focus on small and medium-sized enterprises. The review examines licensing frameworks, sectoral policies, and other regulations that may create unnecessary barriers to market entry, competition, or investment. The findings will inform potential regulatory reforms aimed at reducing barriers while preserving legitimate policy objectives. The Commission also approved the [acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Prince Sub](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20132), subject to conditions.

## **Data governance**

#### **International cooperation**

The **G7** Data Protection and Privacy Authorities adopted a [statement on privacy-preserving age assurance](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20089). The statement sets out seven data protection principles for the design and deployment of age assurance mechanisms. The Five Eyes cybersecurity agencies issued a [statement on the cyber risks posed by AI](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19982). The agencies encouraged the use of AI to strengthen cybersecurity operations and emphasized secure-by-design and secure-by-default principles. They also noted that AI systems may introduce new vulnerabilities, including zero-day vulnerabilities. Finally, the Asia-Pacific data protection authorities, including those of Japan and South Korea, launched a [working group on the illegal distribution of personal information](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19858).

#### **Europe**

In the **European Union**, the [Regulation](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/2075) on horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements came into force. The Regulation establishes cybersecurity requirements for hardware and software products with digital elements placed on the EU market and sets rules for the designation, notification, and oversight of conformity assessment bodies responsible for assessing compliance. Additionally, the European Data Protection Board opened a consultation on a [common template](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19751)for data breach notifications, and the European Commission signed a [Digital Partnership](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19791) with Brazil covering cross-border data flows, AI, and e-commerce.

At the judicial level, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that national courts may use [unlawfully collected personal data as evidence](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19874) subject to data minimization requirements, and clarified that national supervisory authorities may not reject a [complaint under Article 77 of the](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19873)General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) solely on the ground that judicial proceedings under Article 79 are pending.

At the member-state level, the Spanish and Belgian Data Protection Agencies adopted [recommendations for the video game industry](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19908) on personal data protection and children's rights. The Irish High Court upheld the Data Protection Commission's findings and EUR 530 million fine against [TikTok](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/3520) over violations of the GDPR's data transfer provisions, while referring questions on the fining methodology to the Court of Justice of the European Union.

In the **United Kingdom**, the [commencement no. 6 and transitional and saving provisions regulations](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18104) brought into force Section 103 and Schedule 10 of the Data (Use and Access) Act concerning data protection complaints. The provisions establish a statutory right for individuals to submit complaints directly to data controllers and require controllers to provide at least one means of submitting complaints, acknowledge complaints within 30 days, investigate them without undue delay, and notify complainants of the outcome.

The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) adopted the [draft Revised Telecommunications Security Code of Practice](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/16012). The draft updates governance, risk management, and technical security guidance for medium and large public telecommunications providers, reflecting evolving cyber threats and clarifying compliance with statutory security duties. The DSIT also opened a consultation as part of its [inquiry into data intermediaries](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19754). The consultation seeks views on measures to clarify the role of data intermediaries and improve how data controllers handle delegated personal data access requests. Additionally, the Information Commissioner's Office released [guidance](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/15076)for consumer Internet of Things products and services, and the Office of Communications issued revised [network and service resilience guidance](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19844) for communications providers.

#### **Asia and Australia**

In **China**, the National Information Security Standardization Technical Committee opened consultations on national standards on [automated tools for data security collection](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19870), a [zero trust capability maturity model](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19866), and a [personal information security specification](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19860).

The Cyberspace Administration (CAC) and other Ministries adopted[the measures](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17386) for the risk assessment of network data security and adopted [security requirements](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19376) and [implementation rules for cybersecurity labeling](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19374) of consumer-grade connected cameras. Further, the CAC identified [30 mobile applications](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19786) in violation of personal information protection requirements, including failure to disclose collection and use rules, unnecessary device permission requests, and lack of a valid account cancellation function.

In **Japan**, the Personal Information Protection Commission and the Financial Services Agency closed their consultation on [amended guidelines](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19393) for the protection of personal information in the financial sector. Furthermore, Japan–Singapore [memoranda of cooperation](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18900) on the mutual recognition of IoT cybersecurity labeling schemes came into force, and the Japanese and Philippine data protection authorities signed a [memorandum of cooperation](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19628) on personal data protection and privacy enforcement. Regarding enforcement, the Personal Information Protection Commission published a [summary](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19782) of its monitoring and supervisory activities on personal information handling by digital operators, issuing guidance on cases including unpatched vulnerabilities, exposed databases, unlawful collection of pre-order-completion data for marketing, and unauthorized third-party data sharing.

The **Saudi** Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority issued the [Data Monetization Policy](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19962), governing the commercialization of data-driven products derived from government-generated data, and structured around seven core principles, including treating data as a national asset, privacy by design, and preventing monopolistic practices.

In **South Korea**, several bills were introduced to the National Assembly to establish victim protection funds under the [Personal Information Protection Act](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19805) and the [Network Act](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19818), to [consolidate location information obligations](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19872) with the Personal Information Protection Act, and to set [data protection rules for physical AI development](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19684).

The Ministry of Science and Information and Communication Technology issued a [roadmap](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19991) for software supply chain security, including supply chain security standards and guidelines, expanded vulnerability reporting through bug bounty, and coordinated vulnerability disclosure frameworks. The Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) opened consultations on amendments to the Enforcement Decree of the Personal Information Protection Act covering [data protection regulation](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19600), [authority governance](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19601), [reporting and certification requirements](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19632), and [data portability for large-scale employment platforms](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20126). The PIPC also issued a revised [guide](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20019) on the right to request the transfer of personal information, blockchain service personal data protection [guidelines](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20005), and [guidance on credential management](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19807) for cloud services. Additionally, the PIPC signed memoranda of understanding on data protection cooperation with its counterparts in [Hong Kong](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19817) and [Singapore](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19816).

Regarding **enforcement**, the PIPC fined [Coupang](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17328) KRW 624.7 billion, comprising KRW 423.575 billion in fines for a data breach affecting approximately 37.55 million individuals, caused by negligent management of authentication signing keys and inadequate access controls, and KRW 201.106 billion in fines for the unauthorized collection of third-party online activity records affecting approximately 11.17 million users, with additional violations including failure to notify affected individuals within 72 hours. The PIPC also fined [Bithumb](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20004) KRW 210 million over cross-border data transfer violations and announced an investigation into [Tving](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19668) over an alleged data breach.

#### **Americas**

In **Canada**, the [Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/15184) received royal assent. The Act requires designated operators in critical sectors to implement cybersecurity programs, manage supply chain risks, report cybersecurity incidents, and comply with government cybersecurity directions. It also amends the Telecommunications Act to [authorize the government](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/15321) to direct telecommunications providers to take measures to secure their networks. The Lawful Access Act (Bill C-22), including provisions on [government access to data](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19407) and [cybersecurity regulation](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19406), passed its third reading in the House of Commons. The bill expands the powers of police and national security agencies to require telecommunications and electronic service providers to provide digital evidence, user identifiers, and metadata. Additionally, the [Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19838) (Bill C-36) was introduced to the House of Commons. The Bill establishes rules on the collection, use, and disclosure of personal information, including consent, data minimization, legitimate interests, privacy management program, and breach notification. It also grants individuals rights relating to access, automated decision-making, and data mobility. Regarding enforcement, the Office of the Privacy Commissioner found [X](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/13444) in breach of the consent and appropriateness requirements of the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act in relation to the generation of sexualized deepfakes.

Global Digital Policy Roundup: June 2026
The roundup is produced by Digital Policy Alert, an independent repository of policy changes affecting the digital economy. If you have feedback or questions, please contact Maria Buza .
Overview. The roundup serves as a guide for navigating global digital policy based on the work of the Digital Policy Alert . To ensure trust, every finding links to the Digital Policy Alert entry with the official government source. The full Digital Policy Alert dataset is available for you to access, filter, and download. To stay updated, Digital Policy Alert also offers a customizable notification service that provides free updates on your areas of interest. Digital Policy Alert’s tools further allow you to navigate, compare, and chat with the legal text of AI rules across the globe.
Drawing from the Digital Policy Alert’s daily monitoring of developments in the G20 countries, it summarizes the highlights of June 2026 in four core areas of digital policy.
Content moderation, including the European Parliament and Council's provisional agreement on the Directive on combating child sexual abuse material, the United Kingdom's announcement of planned secondary legislation prohibiting social media services for children under 16, the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court's final thesis on platform liability for third-party content under Article 19 of the Internet Civil Framework, Australia's bill strengthening enforcement of the social media minimum age, and Canada's introduction of the Digital Safety Act.
AI regulation, including the European Parliament's passage and the Council's adoption of the Digital Omnibus on AI Regulation, the European Commission's proposal for the Cloud and AI Development Act, the signature of the Pax Silica Declaration by ten additional countries, the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity by 35 countries, and the introduction of Russia's bill on supporting the development of AI technologies.
Competition policy, including the European Commission's preliminary positions that Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure should be designated as gatekeepers under the Digital Markets Act, the General Court's partial annulment of Meta's gatekeeper designation, and the UK Competition and Markets Authority's conduct requirements on Google in general search services.
Data governance, including Canada's House of Commons' passage of the Lawful Access Act and the introduction of the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, Saudi Arabia's Data Monetisation Policy, South Korea's KRW 624 billion fine imposed on Coupang following a large-scale data breach, and the Irish High Court's judgment upholding the EUR 530 million fine against TikTok and referring questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union.
The European Parliament and the Council reached a provisional agreement on the Directive on combating the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child sexual abuse material. The Directive introduces new criminal offenses relating to technological developments, including the design, adaptation, or distribution of AI systems intended to generate child sexual abuse material, paying to access livestreamed child sexual abuse, and the sexual extortion of children. The Council adopted conclusions on preventing and combating cyber violence against girls, recommending that Member States and the European Commission take measures concerning gender-based violence online, including through design requirements for online platforms and infrastructure providers.
Furthermore, the European Commission opened a consultation on draft guidelines for the trusted flagger mechanism under Article 22 of the Digital Services Act and issued the State of the Digital Decade report . Additionally, the European Commission and Brazil's National Data Protection Authority signed an administrative arrangement on the protection of children and adolescents in the digital environment.
At the judicial level, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled that Member States may impose individual age verification measures on providers of pornographic content established in other Member States, while general and abstract criminal law obligations cannot be applied to such providers under the e-Commerce Directive. The CJEU also ruled that Member States may prohibit navigation service operators from rebroadcasting roadside check information and issued a judgment on jurisdiction over personality rights claims arising from audiovisual content broadcast on television and the internet.
In Russia , the Federation Council adopted a bill amending the Code of Administrative Offenses to introduce fines for violations of the rules governing recommender systems. The bill provides for fines of up to RUB 700,000 for legal entities, and up to RUB 1.4 million for repeat violations, for failing to inform users about recommender systems, publish rules governing their use, or comply with the Federal Service for Supervision of Communications, Information Technology and Mass Media orders.
The United Kingdom's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology announced plans for secondary legislation under the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act that would prohibit user-to-user social media platforms from offering services to children under 16, prohibit under-16s from livestreaming, and require AI romantic companion chatbots to enforce a minimum age of 18. The Prime Minister also announced an initiative to require technology companies to implement device-level controls to prevent minors from creating, sharing, receiving, or viewing sexually explicit content, with legislation to be considered if industry implementation is insufficient.
The Office of Communications (Ofcom) published draft amended Illegal Content Codes of Practice for user-to-user services and search services , incorporating encouraging or assisting serious self-harm and cyberflashing as priority offenses under the Online Safety Act. Ofcom also proposed crisis protocol measures recommending that providers prepare protocols to manage risks arising from significant increases in illegal or harmful content during crises and maintain dedicated communication channels for law enforcement. Ofcom also published an open letter to online service providers regarding civil unrest in Belfast, recommending the implementation of the crisis protocol before the formal adoption. Furthermore, Ofcom adopted recommendations on designing for media literacy and issued a statement on the categorization impact assessment under the Online Safety Act. Finally, Ofcom fined First Time Videos GBP 80,000 for failure to implement highly effective age assurance to prevent children from accessing pornography.
In Australia , the Online Safety Amendment (Strengthening Enforcement for the Social Media Minimum Age) Bill was introduced to the House of Representatives. The bill expands the eSafety Commissioner's information-gathering powers to cover age assurance providers and app store providers and increases the maximum penalty for systematic breaches from AUD 49.5 million to AUD 99 million. The eSafety Commissioner issued an outline on safety by design obligations to combat sextortion, highlighting measures including language analysis, classifier tools and removal of image-based abuse material. The Digital Platform Regulators Forum adopted a memorandum of understanding formalizing its operation.
Regarding enforcement , the eSafety Commissioner confirmed that three AI-powered nudifying services withdrew from the Australian market following its investigation into their age assurance measures. The Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) filed a lawsuit against Amazon over alleged unfair contract terms related to the introduction of advertising to Prime Video, confirmed that eDreams and HSK United paid fines of AUD 59,400 and AUD 79,200, respectively, over misleading pricing claims, and issued an AUD 19,800 infringement notice to WeFlex over misleading advertising. Lastly, the ACCC issued takedown requests to Amazon, eBay, Kogan, and Fruugo over listings of banned magnet toys and announced that Temu and Gumtree joined the product safety pledge for e-commerce.
In China , the National Cybersecurity Standardization Technical Committee (TC260) opened consultations on guidelines for the security of applications involving minors in cybersecurity and AI technologies and on a national standard on security testing and evaluation methods for critical information infrastructure. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) consulted on a standard on technical requirements for industrial knowledge intelligent computing on industrial internet platforms.
Regarding enforcement, the MIIT issued guidance on the management of in-app information windows, prohibiting deceptive or misleading prompts such as shake-activated redirects and requiring companies to conduct self-inspections. The State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) and other departments interviewed seven third-party train-ticket platforms over misleading promotion and the unlawful collection of information.
In India , the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an order restricting access to Telegram to prevent alleged fraud and misinformation during a national examination period. Additionally, the High Court of Delhi dismissed Telegram's petition challenging the order. The Central Consumer Protection Authority also fined Physicswallah INR 500,000 over the deployment of dark patterns.
In Indonesia , the obligation to submit self-assessment reports under the Ministerial Regulation on Child Protection in Electronic Systems came into force. Furthermore, the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs confirmed that electronic system providers, including Netflix, TikTok, ChatGPT, and Grab submitted self-assessment results on age verification measures. Further, TikTok deactivated 4.1 million child accounts, and YouTube removed 600,000 child accounts and launched a digital well-being guidebook in compliance with child protection obligations. The Ministry also issued findings on online gambling-related bot activity targeting social media comment sections.
In Japan , the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications published a report recommending measures for youth protection in online environments, including default protection measures for young users, strengthened age verification beyond self-declaration, and mandatory requirements for operating system vendors. The Ministry also opened a consultation on a report addressing issues in information distribution in the digital space.
In South Korea , several bills amending the Network Act on the decriminalization of true-fact defamation , user speech rights , hate information moderation obligations , and the preservation of AI-generated labels were introduced to the National Assembly. Further bills address platform operators' liability for hazardous products in e-commerce and age verification under the Network Act.
Additionally, the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) adopted an amendment to its guidelines on reviewing labeling and advertising, requiring the disclosure of AI-generated virtual persons used in recommendations and endorsements. Additionally, the Communications Commission and other ministries signed a memorandum of understanding on technical cooperation for deepfake sexual crime response, and the Broadcasting Media and Communications Commission announced the establishment of an AI crime response inter-agency consultative body . Lastly, the Commission published the transparency report on illegal filming materials, including sexual deepfake videos and child sexual exploitation materials, covering 83 operators, including Naver, Kakao, Google, and Meta. Regarding enforcement, the FTC rejected an application by Baemin to resolve its investigation into misleading advertising of delivery times through consent decree proceedings and fined Trip KRW 10 million over consumer protection violations in airline ticket sales.
Regarding enforcement, the National Data Protection Authority began monitoring pornographic content providers , app stores, and operating system providers for compliance with age verification and age assurance requirements under the Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents and launched a complaints channel for reporting violations.
In Canada , the Digital Safety Act was introduced to the House of Commons, including content moderation regulation , content moderation authority governance , design requirements , age verification requirements , and user rights . The Act would require social media operators to make child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate images inaccessible in Canada within 24 hours, submit digital safety plans, and, for AI chatbot operators, publish user guidelines on mitigating harmful content and addressing users expressing suicidal ideation. The accompanying Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act would establish the enforcement authority. Separately, the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture directed the Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission to review its Canadian programming expenditure framework under the Online Streaming Act.
At the Second Pax Silica Summit, ten additional jurisdictions, including the European Union, Germany, and Argentina, signed the Pax Silica Declaration , bringing the total number of signatories to 24. The Declaration provides for cooperation across the AI supply chain and coordination on measures concerning sensitive technologies. At the same summit, 35 jurisdictions signed the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity , setting out shared principles on AI governance, cooperation on AI supply chains, and access to AI computing resources.
The European Parliament passed, and the Council of the European Union subsequently adopted, the Digital Omnibus on AI Regulation. The Regulation clarifies the AI Office's competences for supervising AI systems based on general-purpose AI models, extends its enforcement powers to AI systems embedded in very large online platforms and search engines, expands access to AI regulatory sandboxes , including an EU-level sandbox, and extends SME exemptions to small mid-cap enterprises. The Regulation also amends the AI Act's design , quality of service , and cybersecurity requirements for high-risk AI systems, the legal basis for processing special categories of personal data for bias detection , and the registration requirements for high-risk systems.
The European Commission submitted a proposal for the Cloud and AI Development Act. The proposal introduces four Union assurance levels with cumulative technical and organizational criteria for cloud computing services to be recognized as providing sovereignty assurance, verified through self-assessment or independent third-party audits, alongside cybersecurity provisions and public procurement access rules .
The Commission published the draft Code of Practice on the marking and labeling of AI-generated content under Article 50 of the AI Act and established the AI Act Advisory Forum and the AI Act Scientific Panel . Additionally, the Commission closed its call for evidence on the review of the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive , released the EU Open Source Strategy , and issued the Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector .
Germany's Digital Committee approved the bill implementing the EU AI Act. It designates the Federal Network Agency as the primary AI market surveillance authority, while assigning financial sector oversight to the Federal Financial Supervisory Authority. It also requires the establishment of at least one AI regulatory sandbox by 2 August 2026.
In Russia , the bill on supporting the development of AI technologies was introduced to the State Duma. It establishes a governance framework for large foundation AI models, including government powers to determine state support measures, mandate the use of sovereign or national models in specific cases, and set risk prevention requirements. The bill also includes design requirements , security requirements , copyright protection regulations , and a data localization requirement . Separately, the State Duma rejected a bill on the mandatory labeling of AI-generated video materials . Finally, Russia and Vietnam announced a cooperation agreement on emerging technologies.
In the United Kingdom , the Ministry of Justice launched the Legal Services Advisory AI Growth Lab , a supervised testing environment for AI applications in legal services.
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) issued implementation opinions on the development of AI in the information and communications sector, setting out measures relating to telecommunications, AI infrastructure, sectoral applications, and governance. MIIT also opened a consultation on a list of selected typical cases of AI applications , including Huawei Cloud's ModelArts platform for large model industrialization, Baidu's PaddlePaddle deep learning framework, and humanoid and embodied intelligence robot applications from firms such as UBTECH and Leju Intelligent.

In India , the Ministry of Communications established a national working group on AI to coordinate AI standardization activities and to support India's participation in international AI standardization processes. Further, the Prime Minister issued a statement on ensuring the safe, rapid, and efficient rollout of AI, "proposing the promotion of safe-by-design AI systems, developing common standards, testing frameworks, and regulatory sandboxes, and strengthening global cooperation against deepfakes, misinformation, and cyber fraud. India concluded agreements with Slovakia covering AI, the Internet of Things, and machine-to-machine applications, and with South Africa on AI and digital infrastructure. Japan's Digital Agency adopted guidelines for the procurement and utilization of generative AI in government administration, requiring contracted vendors to meet obligations including incident response procedures, data handling and quality controls, and security measures against prompt injection and denial-of-service attacks.
In South Korea , three bills amending the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence were introduced to the National Assembly. The first bill addresses the use of non-personal training data in AI development. The second bill expands the Act's category of AI vulnerable groups to include children and adolescents. The third bill establishes a dedicated governance framework to promote and support the development of physical AI. Additionally, the Ministry of Science and Information and Communication Technology consulted on an amendment to the Enforcement Decree of the Framework Act, which defines AI-vulnerable groups and establishes an AI product and service verification system for public procurement.
The European Commission opened consultations on proposed regulations on multimodal booking and rail ticketing . The proposals would require multimodal booking services to display products neutrally and online rail ticketing platforms to host products on non-discriminatory terms. The Commission also submitted the proposal for the Chips Act 2.0 , including measures on eligibility for state aid-compatible support for European semiconductor technology initiatives.
Regarding enforcement, the Commission adopted interim measures requiring Meta to restore and maintain free access to the WhatsApp for Business API for rival general-purpose AI assistants until the conclusion of its investigation. The Commission found that Meta's fee-based access policy was equivalent to an access ban and posed a risk of harm to competition in the AI assistant market.
The Commission reached the preliminary position that Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure should be designated as gatekeepers under the Digital Markets Act (DMA) based on their cloud computing services. Further, at the judicial level, the General Court of the European Union issued a ruling partially annulling the gatekeeper designation of Meta Platforms under the DMA. The Court upheld the designation of Facebook Messenger as a standalone core platform service but annulled the designation of Facebook Marketplace, finding that the Commission had applied an incorrect legal time frame and had not adequately explained why Marketplace still qualified as an online intermediation service following listing restrictions implemented in 2023.
The Italian Competition Authority opened an investigation into Apple over alleged violations of the DMA's interoperability provisions. The Authority will investigate whether Apple ensures that third-party consumer cloud providers have free and effective interoperability with iOS and iPadOS on equal terms with Apple’s iCloud. The investigation was opened following complaints submitted in April 2025 and subsequent complaints. The Authority's findings will be shared with the European Commission to support its role as the sole enforcer of the DMA.
The United Kingdom Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) imposed conduct requirements on Google following its strategic market status designation in general search services. The fair ranking requirement obliges Google to rank organic search results, including within search generative AI features, based on objective and non-discriminatory criteria and to give publishers advance notice of ranking changes, while further requirements cover data portability and the use of publisher content in general search services.
The CMA also opened consultations on proposed steering conduct requirements for Apple's and Google's mobile platforms, and opened a call for evidence on near-field communication access conditions on Apple's mobile platform. Finally, the CMA consulted on final undertakings pertaining to Getty Images' acquisition of Shutterstock and opened an investigation into eBay's proposed acquisition of Depop .
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) granted interim authorization to the application store settlement agreement between Google and Epic Games on the basis that the interim conduct is unlikely to reduce competition for Australian users. The ACCC further issued a determination denying authorization for Screen Producers Australia to collectively bargain with streaming services on model contract terms.
In China , the State Administration for Market Regulation issued rectification measures against Lalamove pertaining to anti-monopoly compliance, requiring the company to cease algorithmic freight price suppression, refund drivers RMB 120 million in unreasonable fees, cut its commission rate from approximately 11% to approximately 9%, and establish a RMB 50 million driver assistance fund.
In South Korea , the bill on audiovisual media services was introduced to the National Assembly. It would repeal the existing broadcasting laws and establish a unified regulatory framework for over-the-top (OTT) services and content-sharing platforms. It sets out obligations regarding service provision, contractual practices, and the use of viewer data, and authorizes the Broadcasting Media and Communications Commission to order corrective measures and impose administrative surcharges for non-compliance. The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) published a report on algorithm-based self-preferencing by digital platforms, finding that artificially favorable ranking increased purchases of a platform's own product by approximately 34% and decreased purchases of the top-ranked competing product by approximately 32%. Regarding enforcement, the FTC rejected applications by Coupang and the operator of Baemin to resolve investigations into alleged most-favored-nation clause demands through consent decree proceedings.
Argentina’s National Competition Authority approved Telecom’s acquisition of Telefónica Móviles , subject to structural and behavioral remedies. Telecom must divest certain mobile, fixed-line, and fiber assets and provide the new operator with access to roaming and infrastructure. The decision also imposes obligations related to non-discrimination, service quality, and wholesale access.
Brazil's National Telecommunications Agency (Anatel) announced an inquiry into the Internet of Things and machine-to-machine communications markets. The inquiry will examine business models, connectivity investments, network impacts, and barriers to market entry. The findings will support Anatel's monitoring of wholesale connectivity markets, dispute resolution, and potential future regulation to promote competition.
The Competition Commission of South Africa closed its consultation on the review of regulations that may restrict competition and the entry or expansion of firms, with a particular focus on small and medium-sized enterprises. The review examines licensing frameworks, sectoral policies, and other regulations that may create unnecessary barriers to market entry, competition, or investment. The findings will inform potential regulatory reforms aimed at reducing barriers while preserving legitimate policy objectives. The Commission also approved the acquisition of Warner Bros. The G7 Data Protection and Privacy Authorities adopted a statement on privacy-preserving age assurance . The statement sets out seven data protection principles for the design and deployment of age assurance mechanisms. The Five Eyes cybersecurity agencies issued a statement on the cyber risks posed by AI . The agencies encouraged the use of AI to strengthen cybersecurity operations and emphasized secure-by-design and secure-by-default principles. They also noted that AI systems may introduce new vulnerabilities, including zero-day vulnerabilities. Finally, the Asia-Pacific data protection authorities, including those of Japan and South Korea, launched a working group on the illegal distribution of personal information .
In the European Union , the Regulation on horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements came into force. The Regulation establishes cybersecurity requirements for hardware and software products with digital elements placed on the EU market and sets rules for the designation, notification, and oversight of conformity assessment bodies responsible for assessing compliance. Additionally, the European Data Protection Board opened a consultation on a common template for data breach notifications, and the European Commission signed a Digital Partnership with Brazil covering cross-border data flows, AI, and e-commerce.
At the judicial level, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that national courts may use unlawfully collected personal data as evidence subject to data minimization requirements, and clarified that national supervisory authorities may not reject a complaint under Article 77 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) solely on the ground that judicial proceedings under Article 79 are pending.
At the member-state level, the Spanish and Belgian Data Protection Agencies adopted recommendations for the video game industry on personal data protection and children's rights. The Irish High Court upheld the Data Protection Commission's findings and EUR 530 million fine against TikTok over violations of the GDPR's data transfer provisions, while referring questions on the fining methodology to the Court of Justice of the European Union.
In the United Kingdom , the commencement no. 6 and transitional and saving provisions regulations brought into force Section 103 and Schedule 10 of the Data (Use and Access) Act concerning data protection complaints. The provisions establish a statutory right for individuals to submit complaints directly to data controllers and require controllers to provide at least one means of submitting complaints, acknowledge complaints within 30 days, investigate them without undue delay, and notify complainants of the outcome.
The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) adopted the draft Revised Telecommunications Security Code of Practice . The draft updates governance, risk management, and technical security guidance for medium and large public telecommunications providers, reflecting evolving cyber threats and clarifying compliance with statutory security duties. The DSIT also opened a consultation as part of its inquiry into data intermediaries . The consultation seeks views on measures to clarify the role of data intermediaries and improve how data controllers handle delegated personal data access requests. Additionally, the Information Commissioner's Office released guidance for consumer Internet of Things products and services, and the Office of Communications issued revised network and service resilience guidance for communications providers.
In China , the National Information Security Standardization Technical Committee opened consultations on national standards on automated tools for data security collection , a zero trust capability maturity model , and a personal information security specification .
The Cyberspace Administration (CAC) and other Ministries adopted the measures for the risk assessment of network data security and adopted security requirements and implementation rules for cybersecurity labeling of consumer-grade connected cameras. Further, the CAC identified 30 mobile applications in violation of personal information protection requirements, including failure to disclose collection and use rules, unnecessary device permission requests, and lack of a valid account cancellation function.

## **人工智慧**

#### **國際合作**

在第二次Pax Silica高峰會上，歐盟、德國和阿根廷等十個新增司法管轄區簽署了《Pax Silica宣言》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20075)，使簽署國增至24個。該宣言規範AI供應鏈的合作及敏感技術相關措施的協調；同時，35個司法管轄區簽署了《AI機會聯合聲明》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20082)，闡述對AI治理、供應鏈合作以及取得AI計算資源的共同原則。

歐盟議會透過，且歐洲聯盟理事會隨後採納了《人工智慧數位法規》。該法規闡明瞭針對基於通用型人工智慧模型的 AI 系統的監管[AI Office 的職權](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17194)，擴展其執法權限至嵌入在大型線上平台和搜尋引擎中的 AI 系統，擴大對[AI 監管沙盒]的可及性(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17196)，包括一個歐盟層級的沙盒，並將中小型企業的豁免範圍擴展至中小規模企業。該法規還修訂了高風險 AI 系統的設計、[服務品質](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17212)、[網路安全性](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17213)要求，以及為偵測個人資料偏見所設定的法律基礎(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17195)，並調整了高風險系統的註冊要求(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17201)。

歐盟委員會提交了《雲端與 AI 開發法案》草案。該草案引入了四個聯盟保證等級，只要符合[技術和組織標準](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/14100)，便可在雲端運算服務中認定為提供主權保證，並透過自我評估或第三方獨立稽核進行驗證，同時搭配[網路安全性條款](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/14101)和[公共採購規則](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/14103)。

委員會發表了《AI 內容標示與標籤實務守則》草案，依據 AI Act 第 50 條，並成立了《AI Act Advisory Forum》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19598)和《AI Act Scientific Panel》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/15077)。此外，委員會已完成對《數位單一市場指令》中著作權的[檢討](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19386)，發布了《歐盟開放原始策略碼》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17679)並頒布了《能源部門數位化與 AI 戰略路線圖》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19649)。

**德國**的數位委員會批准了《法案》（https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19773），實施歐盟 AI Act。該法案將聯邦網路局指定為主要的 AI 市場監管機構，並將金融部門的監督權交給聯邦金融監管總署。此外，要求在 2026 年 8 月 2 日前建立至少一個 AI 法規沙盒。

## **人工智慧**

#### **國際合作**

在第二次Pax Silica高峰會上，歐盟、德國和阿根廷等十個新增司法管轄區簽署了《Pax Silica宣言》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20075)，使簽署國增至24個。該宣言規範AI供應鏈的合作及敏感技術相關措施的協調；同時，35個司法管轄區簽署了《AI機會聯合聲明》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20082)，闡述對AI治理、供應鏈合作以及取得AI計算資源的共同原則。

歐盟議會透過，且歐洲聯盟理事會隨後採納了《人工智慧數位法規》。該法規闡明瞭針對基於通用型人工智慧模型的 AI 系統的監管[AI Office 的職權](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17194)，擴展其執法權限至嵌入在大型線上平台和搜尋引擎中的 AI 系統，擴大對[AI 監管沙盒]的可及性(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17196)，包括一個歐盟層級的沙盒，並將中小型企業的豁免範圍擴展至中小規模企業。該法規還修訂了高風險 AI 系統的設計、[服務品質](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17212)、[網路安全性](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17213)要求，以及為偵測個人資料偏見所設定的法律基礎(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17195)，並調整了高風險系統的註冊要求(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17201)。

歐盟委員會提交了《雲端與 AI 開發法案》草案。該草案引入了四個聯盟保證等級，只要符合[技術和組織標準](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/14100)，便可在雲端運算服務中認定為提供主權保證，並透過自我評估或第三方獨立稽核進行驗證，同時搭配[網路安全性條款](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/14101)和[公共採購規則](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/14103)。

委員會發表了《AI 內容標示與標籤實務守則》草案，依據 AI Act 第 50 條，並成立了《AI Act Advisory Forum》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19598)和《AI Act Scientific Panel》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/15077)。此外，委員會已完成對《數位單一市場指令》中著作權的[檢討](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19386)，發布了《歐盟開放原始策略碼》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17679)並頒布了《能源部門數位化與 AI 戰略路線圖》(https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19649)。

**德國**的數位委員會批准了《法案》（https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19773），實施歐盟 AI Act。該法案將聯邦網路局指定為主要的 AI 市場監管機構，並將金融部門的監督權交給聯邦金融監管總署。此外，要求在 2026 年 8 月 2 日前建立至少一個 AI 法規沙盒。

在**俄羅斯**，《支持 AI 技術發展的法案》（https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18807）已提交至國家杜馬。該法案為大型基礎模型建立了治理框架，包括政府權力以決定國家支持措施、在特定情況下強制使用主權或國內模型，以及設定風險預防要求。該法案還包括《設計要求》（https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18808）、《安全要求》（https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18816）、《版權保護規範》（https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18815）以及《資料本地化要求》（https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18814）。另外，國家杜馬拒絕了一項關於 AI 生成的影片材料強制標籤化的法案（https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17853）。最後，俄羅斯和越南宣布了一項《新興技術合作協議》（https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19944）。

在**英國**，司法部推出了 [法律服務 AI 成長實驗室](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19809)，一個監督測試環境，用於 AI 在法律服務領域的應用。

歐盟委員會已針對[多模式訂票](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19760)與[鐵路票務](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19759)的法規提案展開諮詢。提議要求多模式訂票服務必須以中立方式呈現產品，而線上鐵路票務平台則需以非歧視性條款提供商品。此外，委員會還提交了[晶片法 2.0](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19646)的提案草案，包括對歐洲半導體技術計畫適用國家援助資格的相關措施。

關於執法方面，委員會採取了暫時性措施，要求[Meta](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17349)恢復並維持WhatsApp for Business API的免費存取，直到調查結束為止，以供競爭對手的通用人工智慧助理使用。委員會認定Meta基於收費的存取政策等同於實施禁令，且存在損害AI助理市場競爭的可能性。

就初步立場而言，歐盟委員會認為[Amazon Web Services](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17167)與[Microsoft Azure](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17169)應根據數位市場法(DMA)，被指定為門檻管理者。此舉基於其雲端運算服務。在司法層面，歐盟普通法院裁定部分廢除Meta Platforms在DMA下的門檻管理員身份。法院維持了Facebook Messenger作為獨立核心平台服務的認定，但取消了Facebook Marketplace的門檻管理員指定，理由是委員會未正確使用法律時間框架，且未能充分說明Marketplace在2023年實施限制後仍符合線上中介服務資格的原因。

### 亞太與澳洲地區  

在亞洲和澳洲，各國競爭主管機關也對大型科技平台的行為展開了審查。例如：  

- **韓國公平交易委員會 (KFTC)** 針對 Apple 的 App Store 付費政策啟動調查，重點關注不公平的排版條款是否損害消費者利益與市場競爭環境。  
- **澳洲競爭與消費者保護委員會 (ACCC)** 對 Google 在搜尋引擎中的商業行為提出異議，主張其可能利用市場主導地位進行不正當競爭，要求進一步審查演算法透明度與反壟斷影響。  

這些監管行動反映了各國政府在全球數位經濟競爭中日益增強的介入力度。

美國競爭與消費者保護委員會（ACCC）基於臨時行為不太可能對澳洲使用者造成競爭影響的基礎，向[Google 和 Epic Games](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19987)之間的應用程式商店合併協議授予臨時授權。ACCC 進一步做出了一個決定，拒絕了[Screen Producers Australia](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19314)與串流服務集體協商契約條款的授權。

在**中國**，市場監管總局針對[Lalamove](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19946)的反壟斷合規問題發布了整改措施，要求該公司停止使用演算法壓低運費、退還司機 RMB 120 million 的不合理費用、將佣金率從約 11% 下降至約 9%，並設立 RMB 50 million 的司機援助基金。

在**南韓**，《有關數碼媒體服務的法案》已提交至國會，旨在廢除現行廣播相關法律，並為 OTT 服務和內容共享平台建立統一監管框架。該法案規定了服務提供、契約行為及觀看者資料使用的義務，授權廣播媒體與通訊委員會對違規行為命令糾正措施並處以行政罰款。公平交易委員會（FTC）發表了一份關於數碼平台演算法驅動的自我偏好報告（[digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20076](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20076)），發現人工優化排名使平台的自有產品購買量增加約 34%，而排在首位的競爭對手產品購買量減少約 32%。關於執法，FTC 已拒絕[Coupang](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19903)以及[Baemin](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19902)的申請，要求其通過同意令程序解決圍繞最惠國條款要求的調查。

巴西的國家電信機構（Anatel）宣布針對物聯網及機器對機器通訊市場進行調查。本次調查將檢視商業模式、連結投資、網路影響以及市場進入障礙等問題。調查結果將支持 Anatel 對批發連線市場的監管、爭端解決，並為未來促進競爭的潛在法規提供依據。

#### **歐洲**

在**歐盟**，《數位政策》[水平網路安全要求之規範](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/2075)生效。該規範針對搭載數位元件的硬體與軟體產品，於進入歐盟市場時設定網路安全要求，並對負責評估合規性的檢驗機構進行指定、通知與監督。此外，歐洲資料保護委員會針對資料外洩通報展開了[共同範本](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19751)的諮詢。歐盟執行委員會亦與巴西簽署了一項涵蓋跨境資料流動、人工智慧及電子商務的《數位夥伴協定》([Digital Partnership](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19791))。

在司法層面，歐洲聯盟法院裁定，國家法院在使用**非法蒐集的個人資料作為證據時**，需符合資料最小化原則；並澄清國家監管機構不得僅因《一般資料保護規範》（GDPR）第 79 條的訴訟程序正在進行為由，拒絕受理依第 77 條提出的投訴。

在國家層級，西班牙和比利時的資料保護機構針對影像遊戲產業採取了個人資料保護與兒童權利的《建議案》（[recommendations for the video game industry](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19908)）。愛爾蘭高等法院支持了資料保護委員會對 TikTok 的調查結果及 5.3 億歐元的罰款，並將關於罰款方法的爭議提交給歐洲聯盟的司法部門進行裁決。

在 **英國**，《第 6 編入法規與過渡及保留條款》（[commencement no. 6 and transitional and saving provisions regulations](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/18104)）生效，將《資料（使用與存取）法》的第 103 節和附表 10 納入實施。這些規定為個人設立了直接向資料控制者提交投訴的法定權利，並要求控制者提供至少一種投訴提交方式、在 30 天內確認收到投訴、迅速調查且不拖延，最後通知投訴人結果。

科技部（DSIT）採用了《修訂版電信安全操作指南草案》（[draft Revised Telecommunications Security Code of Practice](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/16012)）。該草案更新了中大型公共通訊提供商的治理、風險管理和技術安全指引，以應對不斷演變的網路威脅並明確遵守法定安全義務。DSIT 同時啟動了一項針對資料中介的調查（[inquiry into data intermediaries](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19754)），諮詢將釐清資料中介的角色及改進資料控制者處理委託個人資料存取請求的方法。此外，資訊委員會辦公室發布了針對消費者的物聯網產品與服務的《指引》（[guidance](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/15076)），而國家通訊辦公室則為通訊提供者頒布了更新版的《網路與服務韌性指引》（[network and service resilience guidance](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19844)）。

#### **亞洲與澳洲**

在**中國**，國家資訊安全標準化技術委員會針對「自動資料收集工具的國家標準」進行了諮詢（[automated tools for data security collection](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19870），並對「零信任能力成熟模型」和「個人資訊保護規範」開展了討論（[zero trust capability maturity model](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19866)及[personal information security specification](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19860)）。

網路安全主管部門（CAC）以及其他部委已針對網路資料安全的風險評估措施進行了採納（[the measures](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/17386)），同時也採用了針對消費級連網相機的安全要求（[security requirements](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19376)）與網路安全標籤的實施規則（[implementation rules for cybersecurity labeling](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19374)）。進一步，CAC 辨識出有 30 款行動應用程式違反個人資訊保護規定，包括未揭露資料收集與使用規則、不必要地要求裝置權限以及缺乏有效的帳號取消功能。

在日本，個人資訊保護委員會（PIPC）和金融服務廳針對「金融領域的個人資訊保護修訂指南」進行了諮詢（[amended guidelines](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19393]）。此外，「日星備忘錄」（Japan–Singapore cooperation memorandum on mutual recognition of IoT cybersecurity labeling schemes）已生效，日本與菲律賓資料保護機構也簽署了一項《合作備忘錄》（[memorandum of cooperation](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19628)），聚焦個人資料保護與隱私執法。至於執法方面，PIPC 發布了《總結報告》（[summary](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19782)，內容涵蓋數位營運者在個人資訊處理上的監控與監督活動，並針對未修補漏洞、暴露資料庫、為行銷目的非法收集預購完成資料以及未經授權分享第三方資料等案例提供指導。

沙烏地阿拉伯資料與人工智慧監管機構發布了《資料商業化政策》（Data Monetization Policy，[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19962)），規範從政府產生的數據推匯出的資料驅動產品的商業化，並圍繞七項核心原則進行設計，包括將資料視為國家資產、隱私保護設計（privacy by design）以及防止壟斷行為。

在南韓，為了實施《個人資訊保護法》（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19805)）和《網路法》（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19818))下的受害者保護基金，立法者在國會提出了多項法案，旨在將相關義務（consolidate location information obligations）與《個人資訊保護法》整合。同時，針對實體人工智慧的開發設立了資料保護規則（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19684)）。

科學技術部發布了一份[軟體供應鏈安全路線圖](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19991)，內容包括供應鏈安全標準與指導方針、通過漏洞賞金擴大漏洞報告，以及協調漏洞披露框架。個人資訊保護委員會（PIPC）針對《個人資訊保護法施行細則》的修訂進行了諮詢，涉及資料保護法規（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19600))、機構治理（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19601))、報告與認證要求（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19632))，以及大規模就業平台資料可攜性規則（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20126)）。PIPC還發布了修訂版《個人資訊轉移請求權指南》（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20019))，內容涵蓋資料保護法規、《區塊鏈服務個人資料保護指引》（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/20005))以及雲端服務憑證管理指導方針（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19807)）。此外，PIPC與香港和新加坡的對應機構簽署了資料保護合作備忘錄（[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19817)、[連結](https://digitalpolicyalert.org/change/19816))。
